subtitles.text: As Jesus and his disciples were on their way, he came to a village
where a woman named Martha opened her home to him.
She had a sister called Mary,
who sat at the Lord's feet listening to what he said.
But Martha was distracted by all the preparations that had to be made.
She came to him and asked,
Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to do the work by myself?
you are worried and upset about many things,
but few things are needed, or indeed only one.
Mary has chosen what is better,
and it will not be taken away from her.

introParts: Martha did everything right, and still lost something.
She worked for Jesus while her sister sat at his feet.
In this devotional, what Luke really means by “distracted.”
Her complaint is fair. Jesus still answers it.
cards.hookText:
Martha did everything right, and still lost something.

She worked for Jesus while her sister sat at his feet.

In this devotional, what Luke really means by “distracted.”

Her complaint is fair. Jesus still answers it.

Let's watch.

cards.text: Most of us would side with Martha.
There is a guest in her house, and someone has to feed him.
Her sister is on the floor, listening.
Martha is on her feet, working.
In the ancient world, hospitality was counted among the chief virtues.
A host who fed a traveler well was doing something honored, not something small.
And Martha is the elder sister, the one who runs this house.
The welcome is hers to give.
When she is left alone with it, the sting is real.
So her complaint is not petty.
It is the complaint of a responsible woman doing a good thing by herself.
Jesus had just told a lawyer that mercy means going and doing.
Martha is going and doing.
But look at verse forty.

cards.text: Notice how the trouble grows.
It starts as ordinary care about a meal.
Then she looks up, sees her sister sitting still, and her conscience pinches.
The pinch turns to temper, and the temper comes out as a complaint to Jesus himself: do you not care?
The danger is not open sin.
cards.highlight: The danger is not open sin.

cards.text: It is a good thing allowed too much room.
A home, a job, a ministry, a family: all worth doing, and any of them can quietly eat the life out of a soul when it takes the first place.
Look at how Jesus answers.
He does not say stop serving.
He says her name twice, the way you speak to someone you love.
Then he names what he sees: a heart full of worry, pulled in too many directions.
He is like a physician who has found the disease.
Many things are pulling at her.
Only one is necessary.
Not the meal, not the house.
Being with him and hearing him.
cards.highlight: Being with him and hearing him.

cards.text: Then he says something about Mary that reaches past that room.
What she chose is hers to keep.
Food gets eaten.
Houses change hands.
What a person receives at the feet of Jesus stays, in life and in death.
Martha was right that someone had to do the work.
Jesus never denies it.
He only shows her what the work had done to her, and where the better thing was all along: right there in the room, close to him.
Most of what pulls us from Christ is not open sin.
It is service.
And he still says our name, gently, and points to the portion no one can take.
This week, before you begin the work you do for Jesus, sit down and read his words first.

cards.verse: “Martha, Martha,” the Lord replied, “you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her.”

questions: What good work for Jesus has, without your noticing, become the reason you no longer sit with him?
cards.prayer: Tell God, by name, about the many things tugging at you right now. Ask him to have your attention before the work does.

paragraphs.text: Most of us would side with Martha. There is a guest in her house, and someone has to feed him. Her sister is on the floor, listening. Martha is on her feet, working.
In the ancient world, hospitality was counted among the chief virtues. A host who fed a traveler well was doing something honored, not something small.
And Martha is the elder sister, the one who runs this house. The welcome is hers to give. When she is left alone with it, the sting is real.
So her complaint is not petty. It is the complaint of a responsible woman doing a good thing by herself. Jesus had just told a lawyer that mercy means going and doing. Martha is going and doing.
But look at verse forty. Luke says Martha was distracted by all the preparations. The word he uses there means to be drawn off, pulled away.
That is the picture. Not a woman who refused Jesus, but a woman pulled away from him by the very thing she was doing for him.

Notice how the trouble grows. It starts as ordinary care about a meal. Then she looks up, sees her sister sitting still, and her conscience pinches. The pinch turns to temper, and the temper comes out as a complaint to Jesus himself: do you not care?

The danger is not open sin. It is a good thing allowed too much room. A home, a job, a ministry, a family: all worth doing, and any of them can quietly eat the life out of a soul when it takes the first place.

Look at how Jesus answers. He does not say stop serving. He says her name twice, the way you speak to someone you love. Then he names what he sees: a heart full of worry, pulled in too many directions.
He is like a physician who has found the disease. Many things are pulling at her. Only one is necessary. Not the meal, not the house. Being with him and hearing him.

Then he says something about Mary that reaches past that room. What she chose is hers to keep. Food gets eaten. Houses change hands. What a person receives at the feet of Jesus stays, in life and in death.

Martha was right that someone had to do the work. Jesus never denies it. He only shows her what the work had done to her, and where the better thing was all along: right there in the room, close to him.
Most of what pulls us from Christ is not open sin. It is service. And he still says our name, gently, and points to the portion no one can take.
